weekly_baby_facts: Pregnancy dating is counted from the first day of the last menstrual period; this is not a count of weeks since conception.
The pregnancy calendar starts with the last menstrual period. A later dating scan can refine the estimated due date.
An estimated week helps organise your journey. It does not establish a baby's size or confirm development.
Around this stage, a fluid-filled amniotic sac cushions the embryo, while a yolk sac provides nourishment.
The developing brain and spinal cord are taking shape around this stage.
Small buds that will become arms and legs are beginning to form.
The brain develops rapidly, while early eyelids begin to form over the eyes.
The head begins to uncurl and the arms and legs continue lengthening.
A small mouth and tongue are developing as facial features become more recognisable.
The developing jaw already contains the beginnings of milk teeth.
Fingers and toes are separating, with tiny nails beginning to appear.
The developing skeleton is beginning to harden into bone.
Some babies begin thumb-sucking movements that help develop the sucking reflex.
Small amounts of swallowed amniotic fluid pass through the developing kidneys and return as urine.
Fine hair called lanugo is developing, along with early eyebrows and eyelashes.
A developing nervous system supports arm and leg movements; tiny hands can form fists.
Fingernails are growing, and unique fingerprint patterns are developing.
Hearing, swallowing and sucking reflexes are developing around this stage.
The beginnings of adult teeth develop behind the first set, long before either set appears.
A creamy layer called vernix coats the skin and helps protect it in the amniotic fluid.
Babies at this stage can hear sounds outside the womb. Talking to your bump can be a lovely way to connect.
Developing lungs are accompanied by practice breathing movements in the womb.
The arms and legs are becoming more proportionate to the rest of the body.
The body's proportions increasingly resemble those of a newborn, while growth continues.
Babies may react to loud sounds with movement around this stage; occasional hiccup-like movements may also be felt.
Around this stage, the eyelids begin to open. Eye colour can continue changing after birth.
More fat is developing under the skin as the organs continue to mature.
A baby's heart usually beats faster than an adult's. This general fact is not a way to check your baby's wellbeing at home.
The coming weeks include continued organ maturation and building fat stores.
The eyes can begin to focus, with vision continuing to develop after birth.
Babies begin recognising voices from outside the womb. You can share a few words or a song if you enjoy it.
Fat gained in the coming weeks helps babies regulate their temperature after birth.
Skull bones remain softer and separated, allowing flexibility during birth.
Babies often lie curled with their legs bent toward their chest. Their usual movements should continue.
More body fat is developing to help with temperature regulation after birth.
Sucking and digestive abilities are developing in preparation for feeding after birth; this is not an assessment of individual readiness.
Babies can make facial movements resembling smiles or frowns; these are not signs of happiness or sadness.
Meconium, the material for a baby's first poo, collects in the bowel before birth.
A more substantial skin layer helps protect the body and support temperature control.
A baby's usual movement pattern should continue near the due date. Contact your maternity team immediately if it changes or reduces.
Babies born after their due date may have less protective vernix and more peeling skin.
Movements should continue right up to labour. Contact your maternity team immediately for any reduction or change; do not wait overnight.

early.title: Care begins with you
early.body: Rest breaks and accepting practical help can make space for your changing needs. You do not have to do everything at once.

middle.title: A remarkable connection
middle.body: The placenta brings oxygen and nutrients to the baby and carries waste away through its connection with the umbilical cord.

balance.title: Make room for your pace
balance.body: As your bump grows, your centre of gravity can shift. Giving yourself more time for everyday tasks is a useful adjustment.

rest.title: A little support for rest
rest.body: A pillow supporting your bump or between your knees can help make side-sleeping more comfortable.

prepare.title: Your preferences matter
prepare.body: A birth-preferences conversation can cover support people, comfort and feeding. Plans can change with your care needs.

postpartum.title: Support is part of recovery
postpartum.body: Sharing household tasks and accepting help can create more opportunities to rest after birth.

dating.question: How are pregnancy weeks counted?
dating.answer: Weeks are usually counted from the first day of your last period, not from conception. A dating scan can refine your estimated due date.

care.question: When should I arrange pregnancy care?
care.answer: Contact your local maternity service when you know you are pregnant. Ask about your first visit, screening options and how to reach the team with concerns; local schedules vary.

supplements.question: Do food choices replace prescribed supplements?
supplements.answer: No. A varied diet and a clinician-advised supplement routine serve different purposes. Ask your care team before changing a prescribed product or adding another one.

food.question: Do I need to eat for two?
food.answer: Pregnancy does not mean doubling portions. Aim for a varied diet; energy needs depend on the stage and your circumstances. The Nutrition tab gives general references, not a personal calorie prescription.

rest.question: How can I make room for rest?
rest.answer: Short breaks and help with daily tasks can make rest easier. How you feel can vary; there is no energy level you must achieve.

activity.question: Can I keep moving during pregnancy?
activity.answer: In an uncomplicated pregnancy, comfortable activity can continue. Build gradually if you were inactive and follow any care-team restrictions; week alone does not establish exercise suitability.

earlybaby.question: What is beginning to develop in early pregnancy?
earlybaby.answer: In the early weeks, the brain and spinal cord start taking shape. This describes typical development, not a check of an individual pregnancy.

nausea.question: What if nausea makes eating difficult?
nausea.answer: Smaller meals and frequent small sips may be easier to tolerate. Contact your care team if you cannot keep food or fluids down or feel unwell; this FAQ does not assume you have nausea.

safety.question: What matters most for food preparation?
safety.answer: Wash produce, separate raw food from ready-to-eat food and cook food thoroughly. Check ingredients and cross-contact for your allergies; a general suggestion cannot guarantee an allergy-safe meal.

visitquestions.question: What could I ask at my next appointment?
visitquestions.answer: Write down questions about tests, your symptoms, medicines and the care schedule. You can ask how to contact your team between visits; do not wait for a routine appointment with an urgent concern.

bones.question: What is developing toward the end of the first trimester?
bones.answer: Around week 12, the developing skeleton begins hardening into bone. Development continues at its own pace; the calendar is not a clinical assessment.

connection.question: What does the placenta do?
connection.answer: The placenta supplies oxygen and nutrients and removes waste. The umbilical cord connects this support system with the baby.

position.question: Should exercise positions change as pregnancy progresses?
position.answer: Avoid long periods flat on your back, particularly after 16 weeks. Keep activity comfortable and ask your care team about adaptations for symptoms or restrictions.

firstmoves.question: When might I first feel movement?
firstmoves.answer: First movements are often felt between 16 and 24 weeks, sometimes after 20 weeks in a first pregnancy. Tell your maternity team if none have been felt by 24 weeks.

hearing.question: Is hearing developing around this stage?
hearing.answer: By around week 18, hearing and other reflexes are developing. By around week 21, babies can hear voices from outside the womb.

movepattern.question: Should I count a fixed number of baby movements?
movepattern.answer: There is no single daily count for everyone. Learn your baby's usual pattern. Call your maternity team immediately if movements reduce, stop or change; do not wait until tomorrow.

eyes.question: What is developing around week 26?
eyes.answer: Around week 26, eyelids begin opening. Eye colour may continue to change after birth; a calendar cannot tell you your baby's eventual eye colour.

birthplan.question: What belongs in my birth preferences?
birthplan.answer: Consider where you would like to give birth, who supports you, comfort options and feeding preferences. Discuss these with your care team and leave room for changes if needed.

sleep.question: What sleeping position is advised later in pregnancy?
sleep.answer: From 28 weeks, settle to sleep on either side. If you wake on your back, turn onto your side. Pillows may make the position more comfortable.

growth.question: Why does baby growth continue in these later weeks?
growth.answer: Around week 29 and beyond, organs continue maturing and fat stores increase. This typical pattern does not tell us an individual baby's measurements.

warmth.question: What are fat stores helping my baby prepare for?
warmth.answer: Fat gained in the later weeks helps babies maintain their temperature after birth. Your scan, not a comparison picture, is the personal reference for growth.

preferences.question: Can I change my birth preferences?
preferences.answer: Yes. Discuss your wishes and questions with your care team. Preferences guide conversations, but the plan may need to change for you or your baby's care.

nearDue.question: Will movements slow down near the due date?
nearDue.answer: Movements should continue up to and during labour. Contact your maternity team immediately about reduced or changed movements, even at night.

waters.question: What if I think my waters have broken?
waters.answer: Contact your maternity team immediately, even if contractions have not started; do not wait until the next day. Tell them the fluid colour and any bleeding or change in movements.

duedate.question: Is the due date a fixed deadline?
duedate.answer: A due date is an estimate, not a promised birth date. Ask your team about your monitoring and next steps as you approach or pass it.

help.question: Can I ask for emotional support even if I cannot explain why?
help.answer: Yes. You can talk with someone you trust or your care team about how you feel. Support is available; you do not need to force a positive mood.

pprest.question: How can I make rest more possible after birth?
pprest.answer: Ask a trusted person for practical help and share tasks where possible. Rest opportunities matter more than trying to keep up with every chore.

ppfood.question: What is a helpful starting point for food after birth?
ppfood.answer: Keep balanced meals and fluids within reach. Feeding method, recovery and your own health affect individual needs; pregnancy targets are not automatically postpartum targets.

ppmove.question: When can I return to activity?
ppmove.answer: After a straightforward birth, gentle activity may start when you feel ready. After a caesarean or complicated birth, discuss recovery first; ask before returning to high-impact activity.

pppace.question: Should I follow someone else's recovery timetable?
pppace.answer: No. Birth experience and recovery differ. Increase activity gradually according to your comfort and postnatal advice, rather than using the week as clearance.

ppshare.question: What kind of help could I ask for?
ppshare.answer: Help with meals, housework or caring for the baby while you rest can make everyday life easier. Be specific about what would help today.

ppcheck.question: What should I discuss before more intense exercise?
ppcheck.answer: Discuss your recovery, any pain or symptoms, and a gradual return with your care team. The postnatal check is an opportunity for individual advice, not automatic clearance.
